questions.text: In step 5 you apply changes to product_next, but step 8 says live_cursor is the last change_seq applied. Where is that value kept between step 5 and the swap, and is download_catchup_since the same thing?

Step 5 says to apply a change only if change_seq is greater than the change_seq stored on the row. Pages from /sync/products don't show a change_seq in their response. Where does a row in product_next get its change_seq from?
Step 5 and 7 delete a row by id when a change is a tombstone. If a delete arrives for a row not in product_next yet, or an older upsert arrives later, how does the 'only if newer' rule handle that?

Step 1 says it starts when a Wi-Fi connection is available, but step 7 says incremental sync can use any network. Does the catch-up in step 5 (after the last page) also need Wi-Fi, or can it run on cellular?
Step 9 (resync) rebuilds while product_live keeps serving. What stops step 7 incremental sync from running against product_live during that rebuild, and what is last_incremental_at/mode doing then?

Step 6 lists modes that trigger resume, but step 1 sets mode to downloading only after W is fetched. If the app is killed between the watermark call and the sync_state write, or when mode is idle but a resync is needed, what restarts things?
What does a rep see on first install before step 8, given no product_live exists? Also, how is mode idle used when product_live exists and a resync is running, since mode would be downloading?

The server check says 410 when N < purge_horizon. Step 12 says the horizon is the highest change_seq purged. Is a client with since exactly equal to the horizon safe, and who stamps change_seq on a purge (does purge itself create changes)?
questions.about: Server endpoints, resync_required check and Step 12

answers.text: The catch-up position is the same idea as download_catchup_since, renamed next_cursor. It lives in sync_state and is updated in the same transaction as each catch-up batch. At the swap it is copied into live_cursor. live_cursor is used only for product_live, so the two never mix.

Each item in the page response now carries its change_seq, so the row written to product_next has one. This is an endpoint design choice we make here, and it is in the endpoint table. The apply rule in step 5 depends on it.

A delete with no matching row is a no-op. Changes arrive in change_seq order and all pages finish before catch-up starts, so no older upsert for the same id can arrive after a delete. An older upsert is skipped by the change_seq check. A repeated batch is safe for the same reasons, since repeated upserts are skipped and repeated deletes do nothing.

Yes, catch-up needs Wi-Fi. It is part of the full download, and the brief says the full download runs only on Wi-Fi. Step 4 gates each catch-up batch, and it pauses at a batch boundary on cellular. Incremental sync (step 7) can use any network.

Step 7 does not run while download_state is not idle. So the old live_cursor is never used against a rebuild, last_incremental_at is not written during the rebuild, and the 15-minute gate applies again only after the swap. product_live keeps serving reps throughout.

Step 1 fetches W first and writes all its state in one transaction, so a kill before that write leaves the device with no catalogue (live_cursor null), and launch runs step 1 again. A resync (step 9) sets downloading and clears watermark_W in one transaction. If the app is killed after that, step 6 sees watermark_W null and runs step 1. The 410 path from step 5 now also goes to step 9, so there is one resync path.

On first install there is no catalogue, so what a rep sees before the swap is open question 1 and is not decided here. download_state describes only the download: idle means no download is running. It does not mean there is no catalogue. A device has a catalogue once live_cursor is set. During a resync, download_state is downloading while product_live keeps serving reps.

Yes, since equal to H is safe. Every purged tombstone has a change_seq at most H. A client at N = H needs changes above H, and none of those were purged, so nothing is missing. The server defines H as the highest change_seq among purged tombstones. Purging creates no change rows and stamps no change_seq. That server behaviour is listed in open question 2 for confirmation.

questions.text: Step 1 and step 9 both say they set download_state to downloading, and step 1 starts when step 9 has set it. Step 9 clears watermark_W, then step 1 fetches W. Is that the handoff, and what runs step 1 after step 9 commits?

The page endpoint keeps no session and pages are read over hours while products change. A product updated mid-download could be on a page with a newer change_seq, or skipped if its id was already passed. How does catch-up from W end up correct in both cases?
questions.about: Step 2 Fetch one page / Step 5 Catch up

questions.text: The summary says Wi-Fi gate pauses on cellular, but step 10 says retries wait for Wi-Fi. When all 5 attempts fail and state is failed_exhausted, what exactly restarts it, and does the in-memory attempt count start again at 5 on that trigger?

Step 8 says the swap sets live_cursor = next_cursor. If the live_cursor was set before (a resync), is the old product_live fully dropped, and does the incremental sync (step 7) restart at the first launch after, using the 15-minute gate based on an old last_incremental_at?

Step 8 is titled 'end of the first download' but step 9 reuses it for resyncs. Is the swap identical in both cases, and in step 3 with both product_next and product_live as tables in the same file, how does the app read from the right one by name after a rename?
What does a failed_exhausted download look like to a rep who already has a catalogue, and to one on first install? Does anything tell them?

answers.text: Yes, that is the handoff. Step 8 commits download_state = downloading and clears watermark_W and the other download fields, and step 1 then runs in the same process. Step 1 fetches W and rebuilds the staging table. If the app is killed between the two, launch sees downloading with watermark_W null, and step 9 sends it to step 1. The document now names step 1's three triggers.

W is the highest committed change_seq, and change_seq order is commit order, so every change not already in W has a change_seq above W and is replayed by catch-up. A page can read a product before or after a later change. If the page is older, catch-up applies the newer change. If the page is newer, the change_seq check skips the older catch-up change. A product created behind the page cursor is only delivered by catch-up. Overlap is harmless because of the change_seq check. Step 5 now states this argument. The assumption that ids are never reused is an open question.

The attempt count belongs to one request, is kept in memory, and survives a cellular pause, because retries wait for Wi-Fi. When all five attempts fail, the download sets failed_exhausted. The next trigger restarts the step with a fresh count of 5. Triggers are app launch, foreground, Wi-Fi returning for a download, and the 15-minute gate for incremental sync. Step 9 now lists Wi-Fi returning, which step 10 already relied on. The summary's cellular pause is now stated in step 2 and step 11.

Yes. The swap drops the old product_live completely, so no old rows survive. live_cursor is overwritten with the new next_cursor. last_incremental_at is not reset, so if it is older than 15 minutes, which it normally is after a rebuild, the next launch or foreground runs incremental sync at once. That is the right behaviour, because the new copy is only as current as its last catch-up batch. Step 7 now says this.

Yes, the swap is the same in both cases. On first install there is no old product_live to drop. The app reads only the name product_live. The rename commits in the same transaction as the cursor and state changes, so a read sees the old table or the new one, never neither. Step 6 is now titled as the swap for both the first download and a resync. How an already-open read behaves across the rename is an SQLite detail for the implementer to verify.

A rep with a catalogue sees the old catalogue, unchanged, and nothing tells them, because the plan specifies no UI message. Their catalogue also stops getting incremental updates while the download is failed_exhausted, which is open question 9. A first-install rep has no catalogue, so they see whatever the first-download screen shows. That is open question 1. Whether anything tells them is open question 8. The rep table in the document states these cases.

teachbacks.text:
1. Start of a download. The trigger is one of: first install (live_cursor null and download_state idle), a resync, or a resume that finds watermark_W null. The app first passes the Wi-Fi gate (unmetered Wi-Fi only). It then calls GET /sync/watermark, and the server returns W, the highest committed change_seq. Nothing is written before W arrives. Then, in one SQLite transaction in the catalogue file, the app drops any old product_next, creates an empty one, and sets sync_state: download_state=downloading, watermark_W=W, download_last_id=null, download_pages_saved=0, pages_complete=false, next_cursor=W. If the app is killed before that transaction commits, nothing changed and the next start fetches W again. A network error or 5xx goes to step 9 (retries).

2. Fetch a page. The trigger is step 1 finishing, step 3 saving a non-final page, or a resume. The Wi-Fi gate must pass first. The app calls GET /sync/products?after_id=download_last_id&limit=500, and the first page omits after_id. It asks for gzip. Pages go one at a time, never in parallel. The server keeps no session, because after_id is the only cursor. The response is up to 500 items, each {id, change_seq, product}, plus next_after_id and done. Nothing is written until the whole body has arrived and passed the check. A timeout, network error or 5xx goes to step 9. A partly received body is discarded and the same page is requested again.

3. Save the page. The app checks the page: at most 500 items, each with id and change_seq, ids strictly increasing and greater than download_last_id. If it passes, one transaction writes each product into product_next by id, sets download_last_id to the page's last id, and adds 1 to download_pages_saved. If done is true, the same transaction also sets pages_complete=true and the flow goes to step 4. Otherwise it loops back to step 2. If the app is killed mid-transaction, SQLite rolls back, the cursor still points at the previous page, and that page is fetched again. Rewriting a page is harmless. A page that fails the check is treated like a 5xx and goes to step 9.

4. Catch up. Once pages_complete is true, the app loops while has_more is true. Each batch passes the Wi-Fi gate, then calls GET /sync/changes?since=next_cursor&limit=1000. It applies the changes to product_next in one transaction that also sets next_cursor=next_since. An upsert is written only if the row is missing or its stored change_seq is lower than the change's. A delete removes the row if it exists, and does nothing otherwise. This replays everything committed after W, so it covers pages read before or after a later change, new ids the pages had already passed, and deletes. The doc says this relies on product ids never being reused. A network error or 5xx goes to step 9, and the cursor stays at the last applied batch. A 410 resync_required goes to step 7. If the app is killed, step 8 resumes from next_cursor. When has_more is false, go to step 5.

5. Swap. In one transaction the app drops the old product_live (there is none on first install) and renames product_next to product_live. It sets live_cursor=next_cursor and download_state=idle, and clears watermark_W, download_last_id, download_pages_saved, pages_complete and next_cursor. The app always reads the name product_live. If the app is killed before the commit, the old live table and the staging table both stay intact, and step 8 resumes catch-up. Reps see the new catalogue from this point. The device now counts as having a catalogue because live_cursor is set.

6. Incremental sync. On launch or return to foreground, it runs only if live_cursor is set, download_state is idle, and last_incremental_at is at least 15 minutes old. Any network may be used, and it is not Wi-Fi gated. It writes last_incremental_at=now at the start, and a failed run still counts. Then it calls GET /sync/changes?since=live_cursor&limit=1000 and applies each batch to product_live with the step 4 rules. Each batch is one transaction that also sets live_cursor=next_since. It repeats while has_more is true. Deletes remove rows, so reps stop seeing those products. A network error or 5xx goes to step 9, and the cursor stays at the last applied batch. A 410 goes to step 7. While a download is running (download_state not idle), this step does not run.

7. Resync. When step 4 or 6 gets 410 (the cursor is older than the purge horizon H, for example after more than 7 days offline), one transaction sets download_state=downloading and clears watermark_W, download_last_id, download_pages_saved, pages_complete and next_cursor. Step 1 then runs, behind the Wi-Fi gate, and a full rebuild follows through steps 1 to 5. product_live is untouched, so reps keep the old catalogue until the swap.

8. Resume. On launch, foreground, a start after being killed, or Wi-Fi returning, if download_state is downloading, paused_cellular or failed_exhausted, the app passes the Wi-Fi gate. If watermark_W is null it goes to step 1. Otherwise it sets download_state=downloading, then goes to step 2 with after_id=download_last_id if pages_complete is false, or to step 4 with since=next_cursor if it is true. It never restarts from page 1 once it has a watermark. A resume into catch-up that gets 410 goes to step 7. A resume that fails again waits for the next trigger.

9. Retries. For a network error, timeout, 5xx, or a page that fails the check, in steps 1, 2, 4 or 6, the same request is sent again after waits of 2, 4, 8 and 16 s, for at most 5 attempts. If the device goes to cellular, the retry waits for Wi-Fi and keeps its count. The count lives in memory only. If all 5 fail, a download sets download_state=failed_exhausted, and incremental sync leaves live_cursor where it is. Saved data is kept. There are no more automatic retries until the next trigger, which starts a fresh count of 5. The triggers are launch or foreground, Wi-Fi returning (for a download), and the 15-minute gate (for incremental sync). Other 4xx responses are not retried and end in the same failed state.

10. Connectivity and background. If Wi-Fi is lost between requests, the gate sets download_state=paused_cellular and stops on a saved boundary. If it is lost during a request, step 9 applies. Downloads run via a background URL session on iOS and WorkManager with an UNMETERED constraint on Android. The OS may kill background work at any time. Only the in-flight page or batch is lost, since each one is saved atomically, and the next launch resumes at step 8.
gaps: What reps see and can do before the first swap on first install (browse a partial catalogue or a progress screen) is undecided, so I cannot say what the UI does during step 1 to 5 on first install.
What a first-install device with failed_exhausted shows is not defined, so the UI for that case is missing.
What a read already open on product_live does during the swap's drop and rename is not stated. The implementer is told to check it.
How a 401 or 429 or any other non-410 4xx is handled beyond 'not retried, counts as failed' is undecided, for example re-authentication or Retry-After.

What happens when a download takes more than 7 days from W is undecided, because catch-up would get 410 every time. The doc does not say whether the server keeps the window open or the client restarts.

The server behaviours the whole catch-up logic depends on are unconfirmed: that the watermark is the highest committed change_seq, that queries read only committed rows, that purging stamps no change_seq, and that ids are never reused.

The doc does not say how the app finds out the Wi-Fi state changed so that it can trigger step 8. Step 10 only says the OS reports connectivity changes and does not say what the app does with that report.

It does not say what happens if a swap or resync trigger arrives while a download is already running, or how concurrent triggers such as launch plus foreground are prevented from starting two runs at once.
It does not say how a rep is told that the catalogue is frozen during failed_exhausted or a resync, or whether incremental sync should keep the old copy current meanwhile (open questions 8 and 9).
